cards.heading: Trace-to-dataset loop: definition
cards.question: What is the trace-to-dataset loop?
cards.answer: Making the tenancy boundary in an LLM observability platform the product, not the environment, so one workspace holds dev, staging and production for a single AI product — letting a real production trace be annotated in place and pushed straight into an offline evaluation dataset the next agent version is replayed against.

cards.heading: Why tenancy boundary is the mechanism
cards.question: What structural fact decides whether a production trace can become a regression test case without an export step?
cards.answer: The unit of tenancy: datasets, annotation queues and experiments live inside a workspace, so what can be joined without crossing a tenancy line is set by where the workspace boundary is drawn.

cards.heading: How environment-per-workspace breaks the loop
cards.question: Why does partitioning workspaces by environment (dev/staging/prod) sever the trace-to-dataset loop?
cards.answer: Production traces then sit in a tenancy that development-time datasets cannot reach, so promoting a real failure into a regression case requires an export step that is possible but nobody's job — so it doesn't happen.

cards.heading: Reviewer role obligation
cards.question: What role does the trace-to-dataset loop require, and why?
cards.answer: A reviewer role scoped to annotation queues and datasets but not the developer surface — otherwise subject-matter experts cannot annotate without engineering skills, and their attention is the scarce input.

cards.heading: Drift detection as a side effect
cards.question: What capability does co-locating traces and evaluation datasets yield almost for free?
cards.answer: Drift detection — the traces feeding the regression suite are the same traces being watched in production.

cards.heading: Trace-to-dataset loop: adoption reality
cards.question: What did the reported adoption figure show about how often this capability actually gets used, even after investment?
cards.answer: After sustained investment, only about 20% of sixty-plus AI products had an active expert annotation queue — the capability has to be driven into teams, not something that spreads on its own.
